title: Piano Concerto No. 4 in G major
hook: The piano begins alone and softly, and in the slow movement it calms a stern, loud orchestra.

painting.title: Orpheus Leading Eurydice from the Underworld
painting.pairingNote: Orpheus, who tamed the spirits of the underworld with his lyre, leads Eurydice out through a soft, misty wood; writers since the 19th century have heard that legend in this concerto’s slow movement.

facts: Beethoven wrote it in 1805–06, in his mid-thirties, in the same years as the Fourth Symphony and the Violin Concerto. He dedicated it to his pupil and patron Archduke Rudolf.

It was first heard privately in March 1807, at the Vienna palace of Prince Lobkowitz. Beethoven played the solo part at the public premiere on 22 December 1808, in a marathon concert that also brought the first performances of the Fifth and Sixth Symphonies. It was his last appearance as soloist with an orchestra.

The opening broke the rules: instead of a long orchestral introduction, the piano begins alone, softly. Early critics found that strange. After Beethoven’s death the concerto was rarely played until Felix Mendelssohn revived it in 1836.

In the slow movement loud, stern strings and a quiet, pleading piano answer each other. In 1859 the writer Adolf Bernhard Marx compared it to Orpheus taming the Furies at the gates of the underworld. The image is his, not Beethoven’s, but it has stuck.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a gentle, spacious opening (I), a short dialogue between stern strings and a pleading piano (II), a lively dance that follows without a break (III).

movements.heading: Allegro moderato
movements.summary: The piano begins alone with a few soft chords. The orchestra answers in a surprising, far-off key, then plays its own long introduction. When the piano returns, it takes the themes and spins them out in long, flowing passages. Late in the movement comes a [[cadenza|cadenza]] for the piano alone.

mainIdeas.name: The opening theme
mainIdeas.description: soft, repeated chords in the piano, calm and questioning, ending on an open chord.

mainIdeas.name: The orchestra’s reply
mainIdeas.description: the same theme, but in B major, a key far from G, which makes it sound like a sudden change of light.

mainIdeas.name: The flowing piano writing
mainIdeas.description: running notes, [[trill|trill]]s and wide [[arpeggio|arpeggio]]s that decorate the themes.

stops.hear: The piano alone: a few soft, repeated chords, as if asking a question
stops.happening: The opening theme, in G major

stops.hear: The strings answer quietly with the same theme, in a distant, brighter key
stops.happening: The orchestra enters in B major, then finds its way back to G

stops.hear: Restless, rocking triplets in the strings; the music grows quiet and turns to the minor
The piano returns with a free, improvising passage that speeds up and rushes downwards
Piano and orchestra share the themes; the piano decorates them with running notes
The music moves through far keys; the piano plays soft, rippling figures over the orchestra
The opening theme, now loud, in full chords in the piano
The orchestra stops; the piano plays alone, freely
The orchestra returns; a quiet passage, then a fast, strong close

notice: Listen to the first fifteen seconds twice. The piano’s question ends on an open chord, and the orchestra’s answer starts in an unexpected key.
The loud return of the opening theme at ≈ 10:30 shows how far the music has come from the quiet start.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Beethoven wrote two cadenzas for this movement. Pollini is known to prefer the second, the one built on rushing triplets.

movements.heading: Andante con moto
movements.summary: A short movement for strings and piano only. The strings play loud, short, stern phrases all together; the piano answers each time softly, in slow chords like a prayer. Gradually the strings grow quieter, until the piano is left almost alone.

mainIdeas.name: The strings
mainIdeas.description: loud, short, detached notes, all playing the same line in [[unison|unison]].

mainIdeas.name: The piano
mainIdeas.description: soft, slow, singing chords, answering each phrase.

mainIdeas.name: The climax
mainIdeas.description: a passage for the piano alone, with [[trill|trill]]s, rising to a cry.

stops.hear: The strings, loud and stern, play short, clipped notes all together
stops.happening: The strings’ first phrase, in E minor

stops.hear: The piano answers very softly, with slow, singing chords
The string phrases get shorter and quieter; the piano’s replies grow longer
The piano alone: trills and a rising, passionate passage
stops.happening: A short climax, almost a cadenza

stops.hear: The strings return, very low and quiet; the piano sighs one last time

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: A soft, low chord; the finale begins straight away
stops.happening: The movement leads without a break into III

notice: Follow the volume of the strings. They start loud and end in a whisper.
In the 19th century this dialogue was heard as Orpheus calming the Furies with his song. Hear it that way, or simply as loud against soft.

movements.heading: Rondo. Vivace
movements.summary: A lively, dancing [[rondo|rondo]]. The strings begin very quietly with a march-like tune, in the “wrong” key of C major, before the music finds its way to G. Trumpets and timpani, silent until now, join in at the first loud outburst. Near the end comes a short cadenza and a fast, joyful close.

mainIdeas.name: The rondo theme
mainIdeas.description: a quick, march-like tune, first very soft in the strings, then taken up by the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The full orchestra
mainIdeas.description: trumpets and drums, heard here for the first time in the concerto.

stops.hear: Very soft, quick and march-like in the strings; the piano answers and decorates the tune
stops.happening: The rondo theme, starting in C major and turning to G

stops.hear: The whole orchestra, loud, now with trumpets and timpani
A smoother, singing tune
The march-like tune again, soft at first
The tune is broken up and passed between piano and orchestra in new keys
The march-like tune once more
The orchestra pauses; a short solo for the piano
Faster: the theme rushes on, piano and orchestra together

stops.label: Last seconds
stops.hear: Loud, joyful closing chords

notice: Listen for the trumpets and drums at ≈ 0:25. Beethoven has saved them for this moment.

threads.title: Soft beginnings
threads.body: The piano opens the concerto softly and alone, the slow movement is won by the quiet voice, and even the finale starts in a whisper.

threads.title: Unexpected keys
threads.body: The orchestra’s first entry in B major, the slow movement in E minor, and the finale’s first notes in C major all start away from G and find their way back.

threads.title: Who leads
threads.body: The piano begins the concerto, the strings lead the slow movement until the piano wins them over, and in the finale the two share the lead.

threads.title: Saved for last
threads.body: Trumpets and timpani are kept silent until the finale.
